passage: Daycare note, Tuesday Jagdish, two, screamed and dropped to the floor when the hand dryer roared in the washroom. He covered his ears and would not go back in. At sand play he pulled his hands out as if the sand burned. What I did: we now use paper towels with him, and the dryer stays off when he is inside. I put dry rice in a small tub; he watched, then poked one finger in. We will not force the sand. - Swati, caregiver

qa.q: What does the daycare now use with Jagdish instead of the dryer?
qa.a: Paper towels.

qa.q: How can you tell the hand dryer upset Jagdish?
qa.a: He was frightened and overwhelmed by the noise: he screamed, dropped to the floor, covered his ears and would not go back in.

qa.q: Which choice by Swati was gentle rather than forceful?
qa.a: Swati offered a small tub of dry rice and let him poke one finger in, without forcing the sand.

qa.q: How might the other children's day change because of these small adjustments?
qa.a: The room would likely stay calmer, since Jagdish is not screaming in the washroom and can join play his own way.

grounding: A caregiver's note on a toddler who screams at hand dryers and refuses a texture, using a calm setup and gentle exposure instead of force.

passage: In the courtyard of their village house, Harsha spins and spins until she tumbles into the hay, laughing. Then she climbs up and crashes into the hay again. At dinner she bumps her head against her mother Reena's arm, hard, over and over. The neighbours say, "Stop her, she'll get wild." Reena does not scold. She ties a sack swing to the neem tree. Harsha swings, stomach down, for a long time. Afterwards she sits quietly in Reena's lap and eats her roti.

qa.q: What does Reena tie to the neem tree?
qa.a: A sack swing.

qa.q: What does Harsha sitting quietly in Reena's lap after swinging suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels calmer and settled once her body has had enough movement.

qa.q: Which choice by Reena worked better than scolding?
qa.a: She gave Harsha a safe swing for the spinning and crashing her body wanted, instead of stopping her.

qa.q: How do the neighbours see Harsha's spinning differently from Reena?
qa.a: The neighbours see it as wildness to stop, while Reena seems to see a need her daughter's body has.

grounding: It shows a toddler who seeks spinning and crashing, and a mother who offers a calmer, safe outlet instead of force.

passage: Daycare note, Monday. When a child in the washroom switched on the hand dryer, Farida, two, screamed and pressed herself against the wall, eyes squeezed shut. She could not be soothed until we carried her out. Today we turned the dryer off and used paper towels instead. Tomorrow we will let her watch the dryer from the doorway, holding my hand, only if she wants to. — Sharmila

qa.q: What did Farida do when the hand dryer came on?
qa.a: She screamed and pressed herself against the wall, eyes squeezed shut.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when the dryer started?
qa.a: She felt terrified and overwhelmed by the loud sound.

qa.q: Why is Sharmila's plan better than making Farida stay in the washroom?
qa.a: It gives her a calm space with paper towels and only gentle, optional exposure, instead of forcing her through something frightening.

qa.q: How might Farida's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel reassured and grateful that the daycare took Farida's fear seriously and changed things kindly.

grounding: Shows a toddler overwhelmed by a hand dryer, helped by a calm environment and gentle, optional exposure instead of force.

passage: In the courtyard of their village home, Vikas, two, spun round and round until he toppled, then got up laughing and spun again. He ran headfirst into the stack of hay, over and over. His mother, Trisha, had stopped scolding. Instead she heaped the soft hay against the wall, cleared away the grinding stone and sat close by. After twenty crashes Vikas lay on his back, calm, humming, and let her pick straw from his hair.

qa.q: What did Vikas run headfirst into?
qa.a: He ran headfirst into the stack of hay, over and over.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel after the spinning and crashing?
qa.a: He seemed calm and content, lying on his back humming and letting his mother pick straw from his hair.

qa.q: What did Trisha do that suited Vikas's needs?
qa.a: She made the space safe by heaping soft hay and removing the grinding stone, instead of scolding or stopping him.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel watching Vikas lie calm after the crashes?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and reassured that giving him a safe place to move worked better than scolding.

grounding: Shows a toddler who seeks constant spinning and crashing, supported by a safe, calm space rather than force or scolding.

passage: On the beach near Hamburg, Hana, two, would not step onto the sand. She lifted her feet and wailed each time Felix set her down. Her father did not push. He spread a towel and sat her on it, then placed a little tray of dry sand beside her with a spoon. Hana watched. After a while she poked it with the spoon. Then one finger. She pulled back, looked at him, and poked it again.

qa.q: What did Felix place beside Hana?
qa.a: He placed a little tray of dry sand beside her with a spoon.

qa.q: How did Hana feel when she was set down on the sand?
qa.a: She felt upset and uncomfortable, lifting her feet and wailing.

qa.q: Why was the tray a good idea?
qa.a: It let Hana explore the sand gently and in her own time from a calm spot, instead of being forced onto it.

qa.q: How might Felix feel watching Hana poke the sand with one finger?
qa.a: He may feel pleased and hopeful to see her trying something she found hard, at her own pace.

grounding: Shows a toddler who refuses a texture, and a parent who offers gentle exposure in a calm way rather than force.

passage:
Monday. In the mall washroom, the hand dryer roared. Amandeep, two, screamed and clawed at Papa's shirt. Mohit carried him straight out.
Thursday. At home, Mohit switched on the hair dryer on low, far away in the next room. Amandeep peeked, hands on his ears, then went back to his blocks.
The next Monday. In the washroom, Mohit said, "Loud noise coming. Hands on ears?" Amandeep covered his ears, looked, and did not scream.

qa.q: What did Mohit switch on at home on Thursday?
qa.a: The hair dryer, on low, far away in the next room.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when the hand dryer roared?
qa.a: He felt frightened and overwhelmed, screaming and clawing at Papa's shirt.

qa.q: Which of Mohit's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: He calmly took Amandeep out, then let him meet the sound gently and warned him first, instead of forcing him to stay.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel on the next Monday when Amandeep does not scream?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and proud of his son's small step.

grounding: Toddler Amandeep screams at a hand dryer, and calm, gentle exposure helps his body cope better than force.
